18:20 I'm pretty sure that's not what is happening. When they inject the word "bread", they are nudging the activations toward a direction that favors bread-like qualities. Just to be clear: the activations are the outputs across the network's layers and act as an abstract representation of concepts the network learned during pretraining. The activations show different degrees of generalization and detail as we move through the layers and look more like our own concepts in the final layers. So here, we are injecting the word "bread" to manipulate the network's output to use bread-like features, in addition to processing the original prompt. That's why Claude generates text that confirms it was thinking about bread or that bread makes sense in the context. The same applies to the previous experiment: injecting "dust" moves the activations in a direction that includes dust-like qualities. Therefore, when it is asked whether it detected an injection, it describes the perturbation in terms of "dust particles", "fine granular matter" or "dryness". That's what the changed activations look like to the network because those concepts are the closest within its activation space to "dust". 

One more detail: The injection happens before one of the last attention layers and a multilayer perceptron layer, so more processing is done before generating the output. I assume that if you try to inject concepts in the final layer, you get bad output that is much worse than the sample text generated with larger strengths (14:09)

comments.text:
A better test for this "introspection" would be to ask the models to perform a simple mathematical calculation, outputting only the answer to the math equation as well as a Yes/No, single word answer stating whether any thoughts were injected. Not allowing it to output text that is influenced by an injected concept would actually test its ability to "introspect". My money is on that this "emergent introspective awareness" goes from 20% of the time to 0% of the time real fast.

I don't see how this is different from simply asking a LLM in plain words to keep <concept> in mind when outputting.
Everything we type in as words is transformed into concepts in latent space before words are generated based on predictions made in this space.
Inserting a concept of "smelly socks" into this space isn't that different from simply typing "smelly socks" into the prompt. The concept ends up influencing the output all the same.
If your input has the word "chickens" several times, you wouldn't be surprised that the LLM ends up mentioning chickens in it's output. So why should we be surprised when we inject the concept of "ALL CAPS" into the latent space that the model immediately "notices"? The concept we inject is directly and immediately modifying the output, so of course the output is going to mention "I detect a loudness". There's no introspection needed here. Injecting a concept into latent space is just a roundabout way of typing words that invoke that concept into the prompt.

comments.text:
Thumbnails saying things like "becomes aware" not only distort people's understanding of what LLM's are and what they do, but also detract from what's actually potentially promising and important about this sort of interpretability research. The reality is much more fascinating (imo) than the hyperbole.

One of the critical failure modes in LLM's concerns lack of metacognitive introspection of internal representations in ways that can do things like bind referents and then compare that against outputs to reduce brittleness. Often discussion of ways to address this involves newer or completely different architectures entirely, additional modules, external retrievable knowledge graphs, etc. But if there was a way for LLM's to interpret and recognize their own internal representations of received input that was reliably coupled to output quality, that would be much closer to a functional proxy for metacognition. 

And that's what interpretability research like this is trying to probe. What this paper actually shows is that 20% of the time, and under very specific conditions (essentially a "sweet spot" in terms of layer and injection strength, via direct activation manipulation - not something that happens in normal use,) the model does appear to internally detect activation changes, prior to output contamination. Not just post-hoc generate text about them. 

It fails to do so most of the time, and they completely disclaim subjective experience. It would be more accurate to call it task-specific, fragile introspection under highly curated conditions. But that's not really the point. It doesn't really matter if you think this implies "awareness," which is a contingent philosophical question more than anything else. What matters is what if any functional improvements in brittleness might eventually emerge from understanding this better for future models.

Right now, this is just bounded demonstrations under intervention, not broad metacognition. The results don’t show a robust, general, always-on capacity for self-monitoring. They demonstrate narrow, intervention-validated access that is often absent and sensitive to setup, and fails most of the time.

But this is exactly the kind of interpretability research that could lead, eventually, to something closer to a real proxy for metacognition that reliably improves output. If it can be fully understood and generalized, which it isn't clear it can be.
